title: The disease of envy
hookLine: envy eats good deeds as fire eats wood (Abu Dawud)

cards: Dry wood in a fire doesn't get a little smaller. It goes. Log, flame, ash.

A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud borrows that picture: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported to have warned against envy, because it eats up good deeds the way fire eats wood. Not dents them. Eats them.
Strange, because envy doesn't do anything to anyone. It's a feeling about someone else's life, scrolling past. And yet here it burns the envier's own woodpile.

teach.b: Start where the Qur'an starts. Al-Falaq, a short surah near the end, asks refuge from several things, and one is this, in Pickthall's words: "And from the evil of the envier when he envieth." Now the careful part.
Scholars draw a line between two wishes. Hasad is wishing someone's blessing were taken away from them.

teach.h: WANTING IT GONE, OR WANTING IT TOO.
teach.b: Wanting the same good too, without wanting it gone from them, they call ghibtah.

A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even uses the word envy for that second kind: no envy, it says, except toward a person given wealth who spends it rightly, and a person given wisdom who judges by it and teaches it.
So wanting to be like someone good isn't the disease. Wanting them brought down is. You saw that wish early on, in Joseph's brothers, back on day fifty-six.
Then the Qur'an goes one level earlier, to the wanting itself: "And covet not the thing in which Allah hath made some of you excel others." And the cure.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a Muslim prays for a brother who isn't there, an angel answers: and for you the same. The prayer for the person you envy lands on you too. Fire eats wood.
A prayer for them adds to the pile.

how: Muslims seek refuge from envy in Surah al-Falaq, and teachers distinguish hasad, wishing a blessing gone, from ghibtah, wishing for the same good; praying for the person one envies is a remedy often taught.

o: wanting the same good someone else has
wishing someone's blessing were taken away
feeling sad about your own hard times

games.q: the disease of envy — tap the pairs.
p: an angel says: and for you the same

s: the hadith says envy eats good deeds as fire eats wood
the picture is from Sunan Abu Dawud: log, flame, ash.
any wish to have what someone else has is hasad
wanting the same good without wanting it taken from them is what scholars call ghibtah.
al-Falaq asks refuge from the envier
"And from the evil of the envier when he envieth."

games.q: a colleague gets the promotion you wanted. by today's teaching, which wish is hasad?
o: I wish I had one like it.
I wish she didn't have it.
I hope it goes well for her.
games.why: hasad is wishing the blessing gone. wanting the same is ghibtah, and the third is the cure: a prayer for her, which, in the hadith, an angel answers for you too.

practice: Let one name come up: the friend with the easy job, the cousin with the house, the stranger online whose life looks finished and framed. Notice the tightness the name brings, and don't argue with it.
If you pray, ask in your own words that their good thing stay with them and grow; if you don't, simply hold the wish that it go well for them, keeping the name and dropping the comparison.

wordCard.voice: Hasad. Envy; wishing someone's blessing were taken from them. Wanting the same good without wanting it gone is called ghibtah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: envy, wishing another's blessing were removed.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for them. And for you the same. Next, the disease that hides inside good deeds.
